questions.question: What is a topology $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ on a set $\boldsymbol{X}$?
options: A distance function on $\boldsymbol{X}$ satisfying the metric axioms
A collection of subsets of $\boldsymbol{X}$ satisfying the topology axioms
The collection of all open balls of some metric defined on $\boldsymbol{X}$
Any collection of subsets of $\boldsymbol{X}$ that contains both $\varnothing$ and $\boldsymbol{X}$

questions.question: Which closure property must a topology $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ satisfy?
options: Only finite unions of sets in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ stay in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.
Arbitrary intersections of sets in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ stay in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.
The complement of each set in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ stays in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.
Arbitrary unions of sets in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ stay in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.

questions.question: For a set $\boldsymbol{X}$, which collection is the trivial topology described?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{X}\}$
$\{\varnothing\}$
$\{\varnothing,\boldsymbol{X}\}$
The collection of all singleton subsets only

questions.question: Which closure property is required for intersections in a topology?
options: Every intersection of infinitely many elements of $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ must belong to $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.
Only unions are constrained; intersections of elements of $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ may leave $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.
Every intersection of finitely many elements of $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ must belong to $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.
Every intersection of finitely many elements of $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ must be $\varnothing$ or $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: Let $X=\{a,b,c\}$. Which collection is a topology on $X$?
options: $\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},X\}$
$\{\varnothing,\{a,b\},\{b,c\},X\}$
$\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\},X\}$
$\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b,c\}\}$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual open sets, which fact explains why the intersection axiom of a topology is restricted to finitely many sets?
options: $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(-\tfrac{1}{n},\tfrac{1}{n}\right)=\{0\}$ is not open.
$\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(-\tfrac{1}{n},\tfrac{1}{n}\right)=\varnothing$, which is open anyway.
$\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}(-n,n)=\mathbb{R}$ is open.

questions.question: Which statement about metrics and topologies on a set $X$ is correct?
options: Every topology on a set $X$ is induced by some metric on $X$, so the two notions coincide.
No metric on $X=\{a,b\}$ induces the trivial topology $\{\varnothing,X\}$.
In the topology induced by a metric on $X$, every open set is itself an open ball.
Two different metrics on the same set $X$ always induce two different topologies.

questions.question: Let $\tau$ be a topology on a set $X$, and let $\mathcal{P}(X)$ denote the power set of $X$. Which relation holds for every such $\tau$?
options: $\tau\subseteq X$
$\tau\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$
$X\subseteq\tau$
$\tau=\mathcal{P}(X)$

questions.question: On $X=\{a,b,c\}$ take the topology $\tau=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\},X\}$, where a set is closed when its complement belongs to $\tau$. Which one-point sets are closed in $(X,\tau)$?
options: Only $\{a\}$
Only $\{b\}$ and $\{c\}$
Only $\{c\}$

questions.question: On $X=\mathbb{R}$ let $\tau_1=\{\varnothing,\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{(a,\infty)\colon a\in\mathbb{R}\}$ and $\tau_2=\{\varnothing,\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{[a,\infty)\colon a\in\mathbb{R}\}$. Both are closed under unions and intersections of two members. Which statement is correct?
options: Both are topologies, since unions and intersections of two members stay inside.
Only $\tau_2$ is a topology, since $\bigcap_{n\geq1}(-\frac{1}{n},\infty)=[0,\infty)$ is not in $\tau_1$.
Only $\tau_1$ is a topology, since $\bigcup_{n\geq1}[\frac{1}{n},\infty)=(0,\infty)$ is not in $\tau_2$.
Neither is a topology, since $\tau_1$ misses $[0,\infty)$ and $\tau_2$ misses $(0,\infty)$.
